meta.title: Inferno Tactical Map
meta.text: Dante Alighieri, Inferno (c. 1308–1321). Italian text and H. W. Longfellow translation (1867), both public domain.
meta.scale: The globe follows the medieval picture: Hell is a cone under Jerusalem whose point is the center of the Earth, and Mount Purgatory rises from the ocean on the opposite side. Dante gives sequence, direction and a few measurements; vertical depths and ring widths here are interpretive, loosely following the Renaissance reconstructions of Manetti and Galileo (1588).

measures.text: The ninth bolgia is twenty-two miles around.
The tenth bolgia is eleven miles around and no less than half a mile across.
Nimrod's face is as long and wide as the bronze pinecone of St. Peter's in Rome.

levels.name: Vestibule
levels.pun: Naked, they race after a whirling banner, stung by gadflies and hornets.

levels.name: Limbo
levels.pun: No torment, only longing without hope.

levels.name: The Lustful
levels.pun: Swept endlessly on a black storm wind.

levels.name: The Gluttonous
levels.pun: Lie in a cold eternal rain of hail, snow and dark water; Cerberus rends them.

levels.name: Hoarders & Wasters
levels.pun: Hoarders and wasters push weights with their chests, clash, and hurl reproaches.

levels.name: The Styx
levels.pun: Wrathful souls fight and bite each other in the mud; the sullen lie sunk in it.

levels.name: City of Dis: Heretics
levels.pun: Lie in tombs heated by flames, some hotter than others.

levels.name: Ring 1: Phlegethon
levels.pun: Boiled in a river of blood to a depth set by the crime; centaurs shoot any who rise.

levels.name: Ring 2: Wood of Suicides
levels.pun: Suicides are turned into trees; harpies feed on the leaves and cause pain.

levels.name: Ring 3: Burning Sand
levels.pun: Burning sand and a slow rain of fire.

levels.name: Bolgia 1: Panders & Seducers
levels.pun: Whipped by horned demons as they march.

levels.name: Bolgia 2: Flatterers
levels.pun: Sunk in filth.

levels.name: Bolgia 3: Simoniacs
levels.pun: Stuck head-down in rock holes, soles of the feet aflame.

levels.name: Bolgia 4: Diviners
levels.pun: Heads twisted backward, walking in tears.

levels.name: Bolgia 5: Barrators
levels.pun: Boiled in pitch and hooked by demons.

levels.name: Bolgia 6: Hypocrites
levels.pun: Walk slowly in cloaks gilded outside and heavy with lead within.

levels.name: Bolgia 7: Thieves
levels.pun: Bound and bitten by serpents; they burn to ash, re-form, or swap shapes.

levels.name: Bolgia 8: False Counselors
levels.pun: Wrapped in flames.

levels.name: Bolgia 9: Sowers of Discord
levels.pun: Hacked apart by a demon's sword; the wounds heal and reopen.

levels.name: Bolgia 10: Falsifiers
levels.pun: Falsifiers suffer scabs, dropsy, fever and thirst; some rave and bite.

levels.name: Well of the Giants
levels.pun: Giants stand in the pit up to the navel; some are chained, Antaeus is not.

levels.name: Caina
levels.pun: Frozen in the ice, livid, each face bent downward.

levels.name: Antenora
levels.pun: Frozen in the ice with only their heads showing.

levels.name: Ptolomea
levels.pun: Lie face up in the ice, tears frozen into a crystal visor over the eyes.

levels.name: Judecca
levels.pun: Wholly sealed in the ice.

levels.name: Lucifer & Earth's Center
levels.pun: Lucifer, fixed in the ice at the center, crunches Judas, Brutus and Cassius.

path.label: Climbs toward the hill; the three beasts
Gate of Dis shut against them
The Heavenly Messenger opens the gate
Pope Anastasius' tomb; Virgil maps Hell
Nessus carries Dante across the ford
The waterfall; the cord is thrown
A horn blast; towers that are giants

nodes.note: Dante is 35, “midway” through a 70-year life, on the night before Good Friday, 1300.
nodes.it: Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita / mi ritrovai per una selva oscura, / ché la diritta via era smarrita.
nodes.en: Midway upon the journey of our life / I found myself within a forest dark, / For the straightforward pathway had been lost.

nodes.note: A hill whose shoulders are lit by the planet that leads everyone right: the sun. Dante tries to climb it directly and fails.
Light, quick, spotted. Often read as fraud or lust. Dante will later throw his cord to Geryon, the cord he once hoped to catch this beast with.
Head high, raging hunger. Often read as pride or violence.
Lean and full of cravings; she drives Dante back down into the dark. Usually read as greed. Virgil prophesies a Greyhound (veltro) will hunt her down (I.101-111).
The Roman poet appears, hoarse from long silence, and becomes Dante's guide.
nodes.it: chi per lungo silenzio parea fioco.

nodes.note: Virgil explains he was sent: Mary, through St. Lucy, moved Beatrice, who came down to Limbo to ask him to guide Dante.
Virgil says the hemisphere they left is centered on where the sinless man was killed. Commentators place Hell's funnel directly beneath Jerusalem.
The inscription speaks in the gate's own voice. Virgil later notes this outer gate stands without a lock since Christ broke it (VIII.124-126).
nodes.it: Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate.
nodes.en: All hope abandon, ye who enter in!

nodes.sin: Never committed to good or evil
nodes.note: They chase a whirling banner forever, stung by wasps and hornets; worms drink their blood and tears. Heaven and Hell both reject them.
nodes.torment: Naked, they run forever behind a whirling banner, stung by gadflies and hornets; worms at their feet gather up their blood and tears.
nodes.contrapasso: They never took a side in life, so now they chase a banner without end; they were never stirred to act, so insects goad them on.

nodes.note: Angels who neither rebelled with Lucifer nor stayed loyal to God.
nodes.torment: Mixed into the same running crowd. Heaven expelled them, and the depths of Hell will not take them either.
nodes.contrapasso: They were “for self” and stood with neither God nor Lucifer, so neither Heaven nor Hell will claim them.

nodes.note: “Him who made through cowardice the great refusal.” Unnamed; most often identified as Pope Celestine V, who resigned in 1294 and opened the way for Boniface VIII.
nodes.torment: Runs naked with the neutrals behind the banner, stung like the rest.
nodes.contrapasso: If he is Celestine V, he gave up the papacy rather than act, and is left among those who never chose.

nodes.note: The first of Hell's rivers. All four are fed by the tears of the Old Man of Crete (XIV.112-120).
The ferryman with wheels of flame around his eyes. He refuses a living man until Virgil silences him.
nodes.it: Caron dimonio, con occhi di bragia

nodes.note: The ground shakes, a red light flashes, and Dante falls “as a man whom sleep hath seized.” How he crosses is never told.

No weeping, only sighs. Infants, women and men who were good but unbaptized: “they sinned not” (IV.34), yet merit is not enough without baptism. Virgil says he is one of them (IV.39). Their whole punishment is absence.
nodes.torment: No outward pain: “sorrow without torment.” They sigh, and “without hope we live on in desire.”
nodes.contrapasso: They did not have the faith that gives hope of God, so they desire Him without hope.
nodes.it: semo perduti, e sol di tanto offesi / che sanza speme vivemo in disio.
nodes.en: Lost are we and are only so far punished, / That without hope we live on in desire.

nodes.note: Virgil remembers “a Mighty One, With sign of victory incoronate,” who took Adam, Abel, Noah, Moses, Abraham, David, Rachel and others out of Limbo. The earthquake at that moment broke Hell's rock: see the landslide (XII) and the broken bridges (XXI, XXIII).
The great poets welcome Dante as the sixth among them.
nodes.torment: No torment beyond Limbo's own: desire without hope.
nodes.contrapasso: Their honoured names win them a place in the light (IV.76-78), but without faith they share Limbo's longing without hope.
nodes.it: sì ch'io fui sesto tra cotanto senno.
nodes.en: So that the sixth was I, ’mid so much wit.

nodes.note: Seven high walls, a moat, seven gates, a green meadow inside, lit by its own light.
Heroes of Troy and Rome: Camilla, Penthesilea, King Latinus and Lavinia, Brutus who drove out Tarquin, Lucretia, Julia, Marcia, Cornelia, and Saladin “alone, apart.”
nodes.torment: No torment; they live in desire without hope, in the green meadow inside the Noble Castle.
nodes.contrapasso: Virtue without baptism: it earns them honour in the castle, but not the hope of God.

nodes.note: The Master “of those who know,” surrounded by Socrates, Plato, Democritus, Diogenes, Heraclitus, Cicero, Seneca, Euclid, Ptolemy, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna and Averroës.
nodes.torment: No torment; they sit in the castle's meadow, living in desire without hope.
nodes.contrapasso: The best of human reason without faith: it brings them honour in Limbo, not hope.
nodes.it: vidi 'l maestro di color che sanno

nodes.note: Hell's judge. He wraps his tail around himself as many times as the circle a soul must go down to.
nodes.it: cignesi con la coda tante volte / quantunque gradi vuol che giù sia messa.

nodes.note: Lovers who let desire rule reason are blown forever like starlings in winter.
nodes.torment: A storm “that never rests” whirls and batters the souls, driving them “hither, thither, downward, upward”; no hope of rest comforts them.
nodes.contrapasso: They “reason subjugate to appetite,” so a wind they cannot resist carries them.
nodes.it: La bufera infernal, che mai non resta

nodes.note: Virgil names the line of famous lovers: Semiramis, Dido (who broke faith with Sychaeus's ashes), Cleopatra, Helen.
nodes.torment: Blown along in one long line on the same endless storm.
nodes.contrapasso: Passion swept them away in life; now the storm does, without rest.

nodes.note: “the great Achilles, Who at the last hour combated with Love.”
nodes.torment: Carried on the storm among the “more than a thousand” whom love took out of life.
nodes.contrapasso: Love ended their lives; the storm keeps them moving as passion did.

nodes.note: Killed with Paolo, her husband's brother, after reading of Lancelot and Guinevere together. Her husband Gianciotto is bound for Caina.
nodes.torment: Blown on the storm beside Paolo; the two “go together, And seem upon the wind to be so light.”
nodes.contrapasso: They gave way to passion together, so they are carried together forever, joined and never at rest.
nodes.it: Amor, ch'a nullo amato amar perdona,
nodes.en: Love, that exempts no one beloved from loving,

nodes.note: Never speaks. He weeps while Francesca tells their story; Dante faints from pity.
nodes.torment: Swept on the storm beside Francesca; he weeps while she speaks.
nodes.contrapasso: Bound to the passion that joined them, he is never apart from her and never at rest.
nodes.it: quel giorno più non vi leggemmo avante.
nodes.en: That day no farther did we read therein.

nodes.note: Three throats, red eyes, greasy black beard. Virgil silences him by throwing fistfuls of dirt into his mouths.
Eternal, cursed, cold, heavy rain, hail and dirty snow; the ground stinks.
nodes.torment: They lie in stinking mud under an eternal, cold, heavy rain of hail, dark water and snow, howling like dogs (VI.19).
nodes.contrapasso: They made appetite their life; now they lie in cold filth like animals.

nodes.note: A Florentine glutton, nicknamed Hog. He prophesies Florence's civil strife, then tells Dante that Farinata, Tegghiaio, Rusticucci, Arrigo and Mosca are “among the blacker souls” further down.
nodes.torment: Lies flat in the mud under the rain: “For the pernicious sin of gluttony I, as thou seest, am battered by this rain.”
nodes.contrapasso: He lived for the table; now he lies in cold muck under ceaseless rain.

nodes.note: God of wealth, a “cursed wolf.” He collapses like a sail when its mast snaps.
nodes.it: Pape Satàn, pape Satàn aleppe!

nodes.note: Two half-circles roll great weights with their chests, crash, and shout “Why keepest?” and “Why squanderest thou?” then turn and do it again.
nodes.torment: Two half-circles roll great weights with their chests, clash, shout “Why keepest?” and “Why squanderest thou?”, then turn and do it again.
nodes.contrapasso: Hoarding and wasting, two extremes of one fault, labour against each other with dead weight and get nowhere.

nodes.note: Clergy, popes and cardinals, “In whom doth Avarice practise its excess.” None are recognizable.
nodes.torment: Rolling weights among the hoarders. They are tonsured, but none can be recognised.
nodes.contrapasso: Virgil says so: “The undiscerning life which made them sordid Now makes them unto all discernment dim” (VII.53-54).

nodes.note: Virgil explains Fortune as a heavenly minister who turns worldly goods from people to people.
The wrathful fight naked in the mud; the sullen lie under it, gurgling a hymn they cannot say whole.
nodes.torment: The wrathful fight naked in the mud, striking with head, chest and feet and tearing each other with their teeth; the sullen lie underneath.
nodes.contrapasso: Anger turned outward goes on attacking; sullenness turned inward lies hidden under the mire.

nodes.note: “We sullen were In the sweet air.” Their sighs make bubbles on the surface.
nodes.torment: Sunk under the mire, they sigh and make the surface bubble, gurgling a hymn they cannot say in unbroken words.
nodes.contrapasso: They say it themselves: “We sullen were In the sweet air”; “Now we are sullen in this sable mire.”

nodes.note: Two small flames on top answered by a third far off: a warning to Dis that someone is coming.
The boatman. His boat sits low in the water only once Dante, who has weight, steps in.
A Florentine of the Adimari family rises from the mud and grabs at the boat. The other wrathful tear him apart; he bites himself.
nodes.torment: Rises out of the mud at the boat; the other wrathful fall on him, and he turns his teeth on himself.
nodes.contrapasso: His rage has nowhere left to go: torn by the angry, he bites his own body.

nodes.note: Iron-looking walls; its “mosques” glow red from the eternal fire inside. Lower Hell begins here.
More than a thousand rained from heaven. They slam the gate in Virgil's face; he recalls they tried the same at the outer gate when Christ came.
Megaera, Alecto, Tisiphone, bloodstained with green hydras for hair, call for Medusa. Virgil covers Dante's eyes.
nodes.it: Vegna Medusa: sì 'l farem di smalto

nodes.note: Crosses the Styx with dry feet. The damned scatter like frogs before a snake. He opens the gate with a small wand.
A plain of open sarcophagi, heated hotter than iron in a forge. Lids will be sealed after Judgment Day (X.10-12).
nodes.torment: They lie in open tombs heated by scattered flames hotter than any forge needs; like is buried with like, and some tombs burn hotter than others.
nodes.contrapasso: Many held that the soul dies with the body (X.13-15), so their souls lie entombed among the dead.

nodes.note: Ghibelline leader who saved Florence from destruction after Montaperti. He prophesies Dante's exile (X.79-81).
nodes.torment: Stands upright in his burning tomb, seen from the waist up, “as if Hell he had in great despite.”
nodes.contrapasso: He placed everything in this life; now his soul is shut in a burning grave, still proud.
nodes.it: Vedi là Farinata che s'è dritto: / da la cintola in sù tutto 'l vedrai.

nodes.note: Rises beside Farinata asking about his son, Dante's friend the poet Guido Cavalcanti. Dante hesitates and he sinks back, thinking Guido dead.
nodes.torment: Rises to his knees beside Farinata in the same tomb, seen only to the chin.
nodes.contrapasso: Like Farinata, read as one who denied the life to come: his hope is all in this world and his son, and he sinks back when he thinks him dead.

nodes.note: Farinata names more than a thousand in his tomb, including Frederick II and Cardinal Ottaviano degli Ubaldini.
nodes.torment: Among more than a thousand lying in Farinata's burning tomb.
nodes.contrapasso: Both were reputed to deny that the soul survives, so they share the tomb of those who held it.

nodes.note: They shelter behind it from the stench and pause to let their noses adjust.
nodes.torment: A heretic's tomb: the pope it holds lies among the heresiarchs in the fire.
nodes.contrapasso: Drawn “out of the right way,” he is buried with those who taught error.

nodes.note: The poem's own legend: violence (Circle 7, three rings), simple fraud (Circle 8), and treachery (Circle 9), following Aristotle's ethics.
A ruin like the rockslide south of Trent. Virgil explains it fell in the earthquake when Christ harrowed Hell.
“The infamy of Crete” sprawls on the broken edge and bites itself in rage; they slip past while he thrashes.
Boiling blood; souls are sunk as deep as their violence. Named Phlegethon at XIV.131-135.
nodes.torment: Boiled in a river of blood, each sunk to a depth set by the crime; centaurs shoot any who rise “more than his crime allots” (XII.75).
nodes.contrapasso: They shed others' blood; now they boil in it, sunk as deep as their violence.

nodes.note: Thousands of centaurs patrol with bows. Chiron, Achilles' teacher, notices Dante moves the stones he touches: he is alive.
Sunk to the eyebrows. Ezzelino da Romano (dark hair) and Obizzo d'Este (blond), killed by his stepson.
nodes.torment: Sunk in the boiling blood up to the eyebrows.
nodes.contrapasso: Those “Who dealt in bloodshed and in pillaging” lie deepest in the blood they spilled.

nodes.note: Standing apart: he murdered Henry of Almain in a church at Viterbo.
nodes.torment: Stands alone, apart from the others, among those sunk in blood to the throat (XII.116-118).
nodes.contrapasso: A murderer in a holy place, set apart even among the violent.

nodes.note: Where the river is shallowest, along with highwaymen Rinier da Corneto and Rinier Pazzo.
nodes.torment: Goaded by divine justice in the boiling river, which “for ever milks” tears out of them.
nodes.contrapasso: Scourges of the earth and robbers of the highways: those who spilled blood are scalded in it.

nodes.note: Bird bodies, human faces, wide wings. They nest in the trees and feed on the leaves, which hurts the souls inside.
Frederick II's chancellor, disgraced by envious courtiers, killed himself. Dante snaps a twig and it bleeds and speaks.
nodes.torment: Turned into a thorn tree. The harpies feed on his leaves and cause him pain; a broken twig bleeds and lets him speak.
nodes.contrapasso: He cast off his body, so he is denied a human form: “’tis not just to have what one casts off.” His body will hang on his thorn.
nodes.it: Uomini fummo, e or siam fatti sterpi:
nodes.en: Men once we were, and now are changed to trees;

nodes.note: Violent wasters of their own property, chased and torn apart by black hounds.
nodes.torment: Naked and scratched, they flee through the wood; black she-mastiffs catch Jacopo and tear him apart piece by piece.
nodes.contrapasso: They tore apart their own estates; now they are run down and torn apart.

nodes.note: A bush torn by the hunt. He hanged himself in his own house.
nodes.torment: A bush whose leaves were torn away when the hounds caught Jacopo in it; he asks that they be gathered at its foot.
nodes.contrapasso: Like every suicide he is denied the body he cast off (XIII.103-105). “Of my own house I made myself a gibbet”: his body will hang on his bush.
nodes.it: Io fei gibetto a me de le mie case.

nodes.note: Broad flakes of fire fall slowly like snow in the Alps on windless days. Blasphemers lie face up; usurers sit; sodomites keep moving.
nodes.torment: Broad flakes of fire fall slowly, “As of the snow on Alp without a wind,” setting the sand alight. Blasphemers lie face up, usurers sit, sodomites keep moving.
nodes.contrapasso: A sterile plain under fire from heaven, like Sodom's: the punishment for sins against God and nature.

nodes.note: One of the Seven against Thebes, struck by Jove's lightning. Still defiant; Virgil says his rage is his punishment.
nodes.torment: Lies under the fire, scornful, as if the rain could not touch him; still defying Jove.
nodes.contrapasso: Virgil states it: “Not any torment, saving thine own rage, Would be unto thy fury pain complete.”
nodes.it: Qual io fui vivo, tal son morto.
nodes.en: Such as I was living, am I, dead.

nodes.note: A giant statue inside Mount Ida: gold head, silver arms, brass chest, iron below, one clay foot it leans on. Every part but the gold is cracked, and its tears become Acheron, Styx, Phlegethon and Cocytus.
Dante's old mentor, the scholar who wrote the Tesoretto. He prophesies Dante's fame and exile, then runs off like a winner of a footrace.
nodes.torment: Runs with his band under the fire. Any who stop must lie a hundred years without fanning off the flames.
nodes.contrapasso: Their sin was counted against nature; they cross a sterile sand under fire, never allowed to rest.
nodes.it: Siete voi qui, ser Brunetto?

nodes.n: Priscian, Francesco d'Accorso, Andrea de' Mozzi
nodes.note: Clerics and scholars in Brunetto's band.
nodes.torment: Running with Brunetto under the rain of fire, unable to stop.
nodes.contrapasso: Counted among the sinners against nature, they cross a sterile sand under fire without rest.

nodes.note: Three honored Florentines circle like a wheel so they can keep their faces toward Dante while they talk.
nodes.torment: Running under the fire, they wheel around each other so they can keep their faces toward Dante while they talk.
nodes.contrapasso: Counted among the sinners against nature, they are made to keep moving on burning sand.

nodes.note: The red stream drops over the great cliff with a roar like the falls at San Benedetto dell'Alpe.
Dante unties the cord around his waist, which he once meant to catch the leopard with. Virgil throws it into the abyss as a signal.
Each sits at the cliff's edge staring at a purse round his neck stamped with his family arms: Gianfigliazzi (blue lion on yellow), Ubriachi (white goose on red), Scrovegni (blue sow).
nodes.torment: Sit at the edge of the sand, beating off flames and hot soil with their hands like dogs bitten by fleas, eyes fixed on a purse at the neck.
nodes.contrapasso: They made money breed money instead of working; now they sit idle, staring at the purse they lived for.

nodes.note: The image of fraud: the face of an honest man, a serpent's body, hairy paws, a scorpion's tail. He flies them down in wide, slow circles (XVII.115-117).
nodes.it: Ecco la fiera con la coda aguzza,
nodes.en: Behold the monster with the pointed tail,

nodes.note: Ten concentric ditches of iron-gray stone sloping to the central well, crossed by stone ridges like bridges from a castle's moats.
nodes.it: Luogo è in inferno detto Malebolge,
nodes.en: There is a place in Hell called Malebolge,

nodes.note: They whip two lines of sinners marching in opposite directions, like pilgrims crossing Rome's bridge in the Jubilee of 1300.
A Bolognese who sold his own sister to the lust of the Marquis of Este.
nodes.torment: Marches in the file of panders, whipped from behind by horned demons; one lashes him: “there are no women here for coin.”
nodes.contrapasso: He drove others to serve someone else's lust for gain; now demons drive him on with whips.

nodes.note: Still kingly. He seduced and abandoned Hypsipyle, then Medea.
nodes.torment: Marches with the seducers under the demons' whips, and “for his pain seems not to shed a tear.”
nodes.contrapasso: He drove women to his own ends and left them; now he is driven on by whips.

nodes.note: A flatterer of Lucca, plunged in human excrement.
nodes.torment: Plunged in filth that seems to flow from human privies (XVIII.113-114); he beats his own head.
nodes.contrapasso: He says it himself: “The flatteries have submerged me here below.” His words were filth, and now he is sunk in it.

nodes.note: The courtesan from Terence's comedy, scratching herself with filthy nails.
nodes.torment: Scratches herself with filthy nails in the same filth, now crouching, now standing.
nodes.contrapasso: Her flattering words were filth, and now she wallows in it.

nodes.note: Stuck head-first in round holes like baptismal fonts, soles of their feet burning. Dante mentions breaking one such font to save a drowning boy (XIX.16-21).
nodes.torment: Stuck head-down in round holes in the rock, legs out to the calf. The soles of their feet burn, and their legs twitch hard enough to snap ropes.
nodes.contrapasso: They turned sacred office into money, so they are planted upside down, with flames on their feet rather than on their heads.

nodes.note: Mistakes Dante for Boniface VIII arriving early. Popes stack in the same hole; Boniface, then Clement V will push him down.
nodes.torment: Planted head-down with his soles burning. Earlier popes are pushed down beneath him, and Boniface will push him down in turn.
nodes.contrapasso: He makes the pun himself: “wealth Above, and here myself, I pocketed.” He pocketed money; here he is pocketed in the rock.
nodes.it: Se' tu già costì ritto, Bonifazio?
nodes.en: Dost thou stand there already, Boniface?

nodes.note: Still alive in 1300, so Dante can only place him in the future. He was pope when Dante was exiled.
nodes.torment: Not yet dead in 1300. Nicholas expects him to arrive and push him down into the same hole, head first (XIX.76-81).
nodes.contrapasso: Dante holds him a simoniac, so the simoniacs' hole is waiting for him.

nodes.note: Their heads face backward, so their tears run down their backs. Dante weeps; Virgil rebukes pity for the justly damned.
nodes.torment: Heads twisted to face backward, they walk backward, weeping so that their tears run down their backs.
nodes.contrapasso: They tried to look ahead into the future, so they can only look behind; Virgil says as much of Amphiaraus (XX.38-39).

nodes.note: Manto leads to Virgil's long account of founding Mantua (XX.58-99).
nodes.torment: Heads twisted backward like the rest; Amphiaraus “has made a bosom of his shoulders.”
nodes.contrapasso: Virgil says of Amphiaraus: “Because he wished to see too far before him Behind he looks, and backward goes his way.”

nodes.note: Ancient and medieval astrologers and fortune-tellers.
nodes.torment: They walk backward with their heads twisted round, weeping down their backs.
nodes.contrapasso: Astrologers who claimed to see ahead now face only behind.

nodes.note: Dark like the pitch boiling in Venice's Arsenal in winter to caulk ships.
nodes.torment: Sunk in boiling pitch. Demons with hooks and rakes drive under any who surface (XXI.46-57).
nodes.contrapasso: They did their dealing out of sight, and the demons tell them to “dance covered” and pilfer “secretly” (XXI.53-54).

nodes.note: A Lucca magistrate thrown in by a demon who says everyone in Lucca is a barrator.
nodes.torment: Thrown into the pitch; when he rises face down, the demons drive him under with more than a hundred rakes.
nodes.contrapasso: The demons mock him: “It here behoves thee to dance covered, That, if thou canst, thou secretly mayest pilfer.”

nodes.note: The Malebranche (Evil Claws): Malacoda, Barbariccia, Alichino, Calcabrina, Cagnazzo, Libicocco, Draghignazzo, Ciriatto, Graffiacane, Farfarello, Rubicante, Scarmiglione. Malacoda lies that another bridge is still whole.
Malacoda says that yesterday, five hours later than now, it was 1,266 years since the bridges broke. Christ died at 34, so 34 + 1266 puts this on Holy Saturday morning, 1300.
Hooked out of the pitch, he tricks the demons and dives back in. Alichino and Calcabrina brawl and fall into the pitch.
nodes.torment: Hooked out of the pitch by his hair; the demons call for him to be flayed, until he tricks them and dives back in.
nodes.contrapasso: A deceiver in office, he deceives even the demons to get back under cover.

nodes.note: Sardinian officials who sold favors. Michel Zanche's killer, Branca Doria, turns up in Ptolomea.
nodes.torment: Under the pitch with Michel Zanche; their tongues never tire of talking about Sardinia.
nodes.contrapasso: They sold favours in secret; now they are kept under the black surface.

nodes.note: Slow processions in cloaks gilded outside and lead inside, cut like a monk's habit at Cluny.
nodes.torment: They walk slowly in hooded mantles gilded so that they dazzle, but all of lead inside: “O everlastingly fatiguing mantle!”
nodes.contrapasso: They showed a fair outside over a heavy truth; now the show is gold and the weight is lead.

nodes.note: Frati Gaudenti (Jovial Friars) of Bologna who governed Florence together. Catalano reveals Malacoda lied: every bridge here is broken (XXIII.133-144).
nodes.torment: Walk slowly in the gilded lead mantles with the other hypocrites.
nodes.contrapasso: Their appearance of holiness in public office now weighs on them as gilded lead.

nodes.note: The high priest who advised that one man die for the people, crucified on the ground for every hypocrite to walk over.
nodes.torment: Crucified on the ground with three stakes, naked across the path; every hypocrite walks over him, and he feels the weight of each.
nodes.contrapasso: He counselled “To put one man to torture for the people”; now he bears the weight of everyone who passes.

nodes.note: The ridges across bolgia 6 collapsed in the earthquake at Christ's death. They climb out on the rubble (XXIV.19-60).
Naked runners with hands tied behind by snakes. More kinds of serpent than all of Libya's sand.
nodes.torment: Naked and terrified, they run among serpents. Snakes bind their hands behind them and knot through their loins.
nodes.contrapasso: Their hands took what was not theirs, so serpents bind their hands; here even their own form can be taken.

nodes.note: Bitten, burns to ash and re-forms like the phoenix. He stole from a church in Pistoia, prophesies against Dante's party, then makes an obscene gesture at God. Dante says not even Capaneus was so proud (XXV.13-15).
nodes.torment: Bitten at the nape, he flares up and falls to ash, and the ash gathers back into him, like the phoenix.
nodes.contrapasso: A thief who robbed a church: here even his own body is taken from him and given back.

nodes.note: A centaur covered in snakes with a fire-breathing dragon on his shoulders. Not with his brothers on the river of blood, because he stole Hercules' cattle by fraud.
nodes.torment: Covered in more serpents than the Maremma has, with a fire-breathing dragon on his shoulders that burns all it meets.
nodes.contrapasso: He is with the thieves, not his brothers on the river of blood, “By reason of the fraudulent theft he made.”

nodes.note: Cianfa (a six-legged serpent) fuses with Agnello into one monster; Francesco Cavalcanti and Buoso swap shapes, man and snake. Puccio Sciancato alone stays unchanged.
nodes.torment: Serpents fuse with men: Cianfa and Agnello melt into one monster, while Francesco and Buoso exchange shapes, man becoming snake and snake becoming man.
nodes.contrapasso: They took what belonged to others, so they cannot keep even their own shape.

nodes.note: Each flame hides a soul, like the fireflies a farmer sees down in the valley on a summer evening.
nodes.torment: Each soul moves hidden inside a flame along the ditch: “Each swathes himself with that wherewith he burns” (XXVI.48).
nodes.contrapasso: They used their gifts in hidden ways; now each is hidden in fire, speaking out of the flame's tip.

nodes.note: Shares a forked flame with Diomedes for the Trojan Horse and other tricks. Tells of his last voyage past Gibraltar, sunk within sight of a great mountain (Purgatory).
nodes.torment: Burns in a flame split at the top, shared with Diomedes; within it they weep for the horse, for Achilles and for the Palladium.
nodes.contrapasso: Partners in deception, they burn in one flame, and the cunning tongue now speaks from fire.
nodes.it: fatti non foste a viver come bruti, / ma per seguir virtute e canoscenza.
nodes.en: Ye were not made to live like unto brutes, / But for pursuit of virtue and of knowledge.

nodes.note: The other horn of the flame. Silent.
nodes.torment: The other horn of the same forked flame. He never speaks.
nodes.contrapasso: Ulysses' partner in the horse and the Palladium, he shares his flame as he shared the schemes.

nodes.note: A warlord turned friar. Boniface VIII pre-absolved him for advising how to take Palestrina by false promises. St. Francis came for his soul; a black cherub won it.
nodes.torment: Wrapped in a flame whose tip quivers as he speaks. Minos wound his tail eight times round, and a black cherub claimed him.
nodes.contrapasso: He gave “the fraudulent advice” and trusted an absolution given in advance, but “who repents not cannot be absolved.”

nodes.note: Dante, writing in 14th-century Christian Europe, places them here as founders of a schism. A demon with a sword splits each sinner again on every lap.
nodes.torment: Split open from chin to groin. A demon with a sword cuts him again on each lap, after the wound has closed.
nodes.contrapasso: In the poem he explains the whole ditch: “Disseminators of scandal and of schism While living were, and therefore are cleft thus.”

nodes.note: Curio, who urged Caesar across the Rubicon, has his tongue cut out.
nodes.torment: Throat pierced, nose cut off below the brows, one ear left; beside him Curio, his tongue slit in his windpipe.
nodes.contrapasso: They divided others with words, and the cuts fall on the organs of speech: throat, ear, tongue.

nodes.note: Both hands cut off. His advice (“a thing done has an end”) started the Guelph–Ghibelline feud in Florence. One of the five Ciacco named.
nodes.torment: Both hands cut off; he lifts the stumps, and the blood stains his face.
nodes.contrapasso: His words “A thing done has an end” split Florence into factions; now he is cut too.

nodes.note: Carries his severed head like a lantern; he turned the Young King against his father Henry II. The poem's clearest statement of contrapasso.
nodes.torment: A headless trunk walking with the rest, holding his severed head by the hair like a lantern.
nodes.contrapasso: He says it himself: “Because I parted persons so united, Parted do I now bear my brain.” He calls it “the counterpoise.”
nodes.it: Così s'osserva in me lo contrapasso.
nodes.en: Thus is observed in me the counterpoise.

nodes.note: Dante's father's cousin, murdered and never avenged. He points angrily at Dante and walks off.
nodes.torment: Among the sowers of discord under the same sword (XXVIII.37-42); he points at Dante and threatens him with his finger.
nodes.contrapasso: The ditch's rule holds for him: those who sowed division “therefore are cleft thus” (XXVIII.36).

nodes.note: Alchemists propped against each other, scratching scabs off like a knife scaling fish. The whole ditch is a plague hospital.
nodes.torment: Covered in scabs, they sit propped against each other and tear at themselves with their nails, as a knife scales a fish; the ditch is a hospital of every disease.
nodes.contrapasso: They falsified metals, corrupting matter; now their own bodies are corrupted.

nodes.note: Impersonators running rabid. Schicchi posed as dead Buoso Donati to forge a will and won a prize mare.
nodes.torment: Runs naked and rabid, biting others like a boar let out of its sty; he seizes Capocchio by the neck.
nodes.contrapasso: They falsified their own persons, Schicchi as Buoso and Myrrha “By counterfeiting of another’s form”; now they run mad, out of themselves.

nodes.note: Counterfeited Florentine gold florins. Swollen with dropsy, he dreams of the streams of the Casentino. He gives the bolgia's size (XXX.86-87).
nodes.torment: Swollen with dropsy into the shape of a lute, lips parted with thirst. He dreams of the cold streams of the Casentino, which dry him more than the disease.
nodes.contrapasso: “I had while living much of what I wished, And now, alas! a drop of water crave.” He corrupted the coinage; now his own body is corrupted.

nodes.note: Liars burning with fever. Sinon (who talked Troy into the horse) brawls with Master Adam.
nodes.torment: Burns with an acute fever that sends out a reek; he and Master Adam trade blows and insults.
nodes.contrapasso: They told lies that inflamed others; now they burn with fever.

nodes.note: Louder than the horn Roland blew at Roncesvalles.
Builder of Babel. His face is as long as St. Peter's bronze pinecone; he speaks a language no one understands.
nodes.torment: Fixed in the well “From navel downward” (XXXI.33), shouting words that make sense to no one.
nodes.contrapasso: Virgil: “He doth himself accuse.” Through him “One language in the world is not still used,” so now “even such to him is every language As his to others.”
nodes.it: Raphèl maì amècche zabì almi

nodes.note: Chained five times around; he fought the gods. Briareus is said to stand farther off.
nodes.torment: Chained in the well, his right arm pinned behind and the left in front, the chain wound five times around him from the neck down.
nodes.contrapasso: He tested his strength against Jove, “whence he has such a guerdon”: “The arms he wielded never more he moves.”

nodes.note: Unchained because he did not fight the gods. He picks them up and sets them on the ice, bending like the leaning Garisenda tower in Bologna.
nodes.torment: Fixed in the well like the others, but unbound and able to speak (XXXI.100-101).
nodes.contrapasso: He was not at the giants' war against the gods (XXXI.119-121), and he is the one left unchained.

nodes.note: A lake frozen so hard it looks like glass; it would not crack if a mountain fell on it. Lucifer's wings keep it frozen (XXXIV.46-52).
nodes.torment: Frozen in a lake of ice, livid up to the face, teeth chattering like storks, each face bent down.
nodes.contrapasso: Treachery betrays bonds of love and trust, and is punished in ice, far from all warmth.

nodes.note: Napoleone and Alessandro killed each other over their inheritance. Frozen face to face, butting like goats.
nodes.torment: Frozen face to face; their tears freeze their eyes shut, and they butt each other like two goats.
nodes.contrapasso: “They from one body came,” and killed each other; now they are frozen together, still butting in anger.

nodes.note: Mordred, whose chest Arthur pierced so light shone through. Camicion de' Pazzi waits for his kinsman Carlino to make him look better.
nodes.torment: Frozen in Caina's ice with their faces bent down.
nodes.contrapasso: Traitors to their own kin, frozen in the zone named after Cain.

nodes.note: Betrayed the Florentine Guelphs at Montaperti. Dante kicks his face and pulls his hair; he names others: Buoso da Duera, Beccheria, Soldanieri, Ganelon, Tebaldello.
nodes.torment: Frozen in the ice with only his head out. Dante strikes his face with his foot and pulls out his hair when he will not give his name.
nodes.contrapasso: He betrayed his side in secret; here he tries to keep his name hidden, and another traitor gives it away (XXXII.106-108).

nodes.note: Gnaws Archbishop Ruggieri's skull. Sealed in a Pisan tower with his sons and grandsons, he watched them starve.
nodes.torment: Frozen in one hole with Archbishop Ruggieri, he gnaws the back of his skull, “even as bread through hunger is devoured.”
nodes.contrapasso: Two traitors locked together: the one who was starved feeds on the one who starved him.
nodes.it: Poscia, più che 'l dolor, poté 'l digiuno.
nodes.en: Then hunger did what sorrow could not do.

nodes.note: Ugolino's betrayer, now his meal.
nodes.torment: Frozen beneath Ugolino, his skull gnawed from behind.
nodes.contrapasso: He betrayed Ugolino and starved him with his sons; now he is Ugolino's food.

nodes.note: Had his guests murdered at dessert: he of “the fruit of the bad garden.” His soul fell here while a demon runs his still-living body on earth.
nodes.torment: Lies face up in the ice, his tears frozen over his eyes. His soul fell here while a demon still runs his living body.
nodes.contrapasso: He served death at a feast, and says that here he gets a date for his fig, paid back richer than he gave (XXXIII.119-120).

nodes.note: Murdered his father-in-law Michel Zanche at a banquet. Still walking around Genoa in 1300, but his soul has been here for years.
nodes.torment: His soul is in the ice, while a demon in his body still “eats, and drinks, and sleeps, and puts on clothes” in Genoa.
nodes.contrapasso: He murdered a guest, and his soul fell here before his victim's even reached the pitch (XXXIII.142-147).

nodes.note: Faces turned up; their first tears freeze into crystal visors so grief turns back inside.
nodes.torment: They lie face up in the ice; their first tears freeze into “a crystal visor,” so grief turns inward and grows.
nodes.contrapasso: They betrayed guests who trusted them openly; now they cannot even weep, and their grief turns back on itself.

nodes.note: Completely covered, showing through like straw in glass: lying, standing, head-down, bent like bows.
nodes.torment: Wholly covered by the ice, showing through like straws in glass: some lying, some upright, some head down, some bent like bows.
nodes.contrapasso: They betrayed their lords and benefactors, the deepest trust; nothing of them is left free.

nodes.note: Chest-deep in the ice. Three faces (red, yellow-white, black), six bat wings making the freezing wind, weeping from six eyes.
nodes.torment: Fixed in the ice from mid-breast down. His six wings beat out the wind that freezes it, and he weeps from six eyes while chewing three traitors.
nodes.contrapasso: He rebelled to rise above God and is fixed at the point farthest from Him, frozen by his own wings.
nodes.it: Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni / verso di noi; però dinanzi mira
nodes.en: Vexilla Regis prodeunt Inferni / Towards us; therefore look in front of thee

nodes.note: In the front mouth, head inside, legs kicking; his back flayed by claws.
nodes.torment: In Lucifer's front mouth, head inside and legs kicking; the claws strip the skin from his back. Virgil calls it “the greatest pain.”
nodes.contrapasso: The betrayer of Christ has the worst place: head first in the mouth of the first rebel.

nodes.note: Hangs from the black face, writhing without a word.
nodes.torment: Hangs head down from Lucifer's black face, writhing and saying nothing.
nodes.contrapasso: He betrayed Caesar, his benefactor and, for Dante, the founder of the empire; he is chewed by the first traitor.

nodes.note: The one “who so stalwart seems,” in the third mouth.
nodes.torment: Hangs head down from the third mouth, he “who so stalwart seems.”
nodes.contrapasso: Brutus's partner in killing Caesar, he shares Lucifer's jaws with him.

nodes.note: At Lucifer's hip Virgil turns head-to-feet: they pass “the point To which things heavy draw from every side.” Down becomes up.
nodes.it: 'l punto / al qual si traggon d'ogne parte i pesi.

nodes.note: When he fell from heaven, the land fled from him to the north; the displaced earth rushed up to form the mountain of Purgatory.
Following a little stream up a hidden passage, they come out under the stars. Each of the three canticles ends on the word stelle.
nodes.it: E quindi uscimmo a riveder le stelle.
nodes.en: Thence we came forth to rebehold the stars.

edges.note: “Caina waits for him who quenched our life”: her husband Gianciotto
Christ broke the outer gate; it stays unlocked
The same quake broke the bridges of bolgia 6
Malacoda lied that another bridge was whole
The cord Dante meant to snare the leopard with
Thrown into the abyss, it summons Geryon
Nicholas expects Boniface to replace him in the hole
Minos wraps his tail eight times for Guido
One flame, split at the top
He drowned in sight of the mountain
Dante says not even Capaneus was this proud against God
A centaur kept apart from his brothers for fraud
Schicchi impersonated Buoso Donati; many commentators read the Buoso among the thieves as the same family
Virgil went down this far once before, summoned by the witch Erichtho
Beatrice came to Limbo to send Virgil
His fall pushed up the mountain
Celestine's resignation made way for Boniface

tableaux.note: The lustful are driven round and round by the infernal storm; the direction, speed and spacing are staging.
A second stream swept the other way round the same ring, as the storm tosses them up and down; staging.
Cold, heavy, accursed rain and hail pour down without pause; the number of drops and their speed are staging.
The gluttons lie in the foul mire under the rain; where they lie and how they stir is staging.
Cerberus tears and flays the souls with his claws; his place on the ring and his movement are staging.
The simoniacs are fixed head-down in round holes in the rock; their number and spacing are staging.
Fire plays over the soles of their feet as they kick; the flicker is staging.
Caina: the traitors to kin are frozen to the neck, heads bent; their stillness is the poem, the tiny shiver is staging.
Antenora: the traitors to country, frozen with faces upright; the shiver is staging.
Ptolomea: the traitors to guests lie face up, their tears freezing in their eyes; the shiver is staging.
Judecca: the traitors to their benefactors are wholly covered in the ice; the glint is staging.
The river of the threshold; the poem gives the river, the flow is staging.
The marsh of the Styx; the flow is staging.
The sullen sunk in the mud and bubbling up; the bubbling rate is staging.
The tombs burn; where the flames stand and how they flicker is staging.
The diviners walk backwards with their heads twisted round, so their tears run down their backs; the pace is staging.
A lake of boiling pitch; the bubbling is staging.
A slow procession in gilded leaden cloaks; the pace is staging.
Serpents swarm over the thieves; their speed and spacing are staging.
Each flame hides a sinner, seen like fireflies in the dark; the flicker is staging.
The sowers of discord circle the ditch and are split open by a sword each lap; the pace is staging.
The river of boiling blood flows round the ring; the poem gives the river, the speed and direction are staging.
Boiling blood; the bubbling is staging.
The violent against others, sunk in the blood to different depths by their guilt; the poem gives the depths, the bobbing is staging.
Centaurs run along the bank shooting at any soul that rises out of the blood further than its guilt allows; their pace and number here are staging.

One half-circle of hoarders rolls great weights with their chests; the poem has them clash with the opposite half and turn back. Clerics are marked among them (VII.46-48). Pace and spacing are staging.
The opposite half-circle, the wasters, meets the hoarders at the clash and turns back; the second clash point lies inside the cut wedge.
Virgil throws the cord into the abyss as a signal; the poem states the throw, the timing against the journey bar is staging.
Geryon comes up out of the abyss, waits on the ledge, then carries them down in slow circles (XVII.115-117) to the first bolgia; the sequence is from the poem, the keyframes are staging.
The red stream drops over the great cliff into the eighth circle; the poem gives the fall and its roar, the width and mist are staging.
Two files of the pandering and seduced, walking in opposite directions along the ditch; the poem states the opposed directions, the pace and spacing are staging.
The opposite file, seen as 'coming toward us' in the poem.
Horned demons with great whips lash the walkers; where they stand is staging.
